## Introduction {#introduction}

Artificial intelligence (AI) models are increasingly being used to assist with or automate tasks that have traditionally relied on human annotation and expert judgment. Examples include interpreting medical images [@aggarwal2021diagnostic], identifying harmful or toxic online content [@gorwa2020algorithmic], and evaluating or ranking generated responses [@ouyang2022training]. For these tasks, human annotations often provide the supervision used to train the models [@prabhakaran2024grasp; @uma2021learning].

However, these tasks are usually subjective, so the labels used to train a model depend on the judgments of the human annotators. For example, annotators may disagree about whether a text contains hate speech or which emotion it expresses [@rottger2022two; @davani2022dealing]. Human preferences also enter language-model training through demonstrations and comparisons between responses, as in InstructGPT [@ouyang2022training]. A related issue arises in medical imaging: radiologists may disagree about findings in the same chest X-ray, so the reference label can depend on which radiologists assess it [@abdalla2023hurdles]. 
When annotators' judgments leave consistent patterns in the labels they provide, this is commonly referred to as *annotation bias* [@geva2019we; @wich-etal-2020-investigating].

Such systematic bias in annotation can affect the performance comparisons between trained models and human annotators (hereafter *model–human comparisons*). These comparisons have attracted considerable attention in medical imaging [@liu2019comparison; @nagendran2020artificial; @ahmad2023machine]. For example, in chest X-ray interpretation, @irvin2019chexpert reports that its model outperformed individual radiologists on several findings, while @wu2020comparison reports higher specificity and precision for an AI model than for radiology residents. Both studies used reference labels established by panels of specialists through majority voting or consensus. However, the former study did not report whether the training annotators overlapped with the reference experts, while in the latter, one of the reference experts was also involved in training. Now we use a simple model to explain how annotation bias can affect model–human comparisons under this overlap.

Denote the label given by an annotator $i$ on object $x$ as $Y_i(x)$ and the corresponding latent truth as $Y^*(x)$, we write
$$Y_i(x) = Y^*(x) + b_i(x) + \epsilon_{i,x},$$
where $b_i(x)$ is the systematic bias of annotator $i$ and $\epsilon_{i,x}$ is the noise. Suppose a model $\widehat Y_A$ is trained on annotator A and compared with annotator B. Assume the reference is again the annotator A and the comparison is on dataset $\mathcal{D}$. Then the model–human comparison is between 
$\sum_{x \in \mathcal{D}} || \widehat Y_A (x) - Y_A (x) ||$ and $\sum_{x \in \mathcal{D}} || Y_B (x) - Y_A (x) ||,$
which can also be written as
$$ \sum_{x \in \mathcal{D}} || \widehat e_A (x) - \epsilon_{A,x} || \quad \mathrm{versus} \quad  \sum_{x \in \mathcal{D}} ||\big(b_B(x) - b_A(x)\big) + \epsilon_{B,x} - \epsilon_{A,x}||.$$ {#eq-intro-self-ref}
Here $\widehat e_A (x)$ captures the approximation error and training error arising from finite samples and incomplete optimization, and the rewrite holds under mild conditions^[Sufficient conditions are that $\mathbb{E}[\epsilon_{A,x}\mid x]=0$ and that MSE is used as the training loss.]. 
Similarly, when the latent truth is chosen as the reference, we can rewrite the actual model–human comparison, between $\sum_{x \in \mathcal{D}} ||\widehat Y_A (x) - Y^*(x)||$ and $\sum_{x \in \mathcal{D}} ||Y_B (x) - Y^*(x)||$ as
$$ \sum_{x \in \mathcal{D}} || \widehat e_A (x) + b_A(x) || \quad \mathrm{versus} \quad  \sum_{x \in \mathcal{D}} ||b_B(x) + \epsilon_{B,x} ||.$$ {#eq-intro-latent-ref}
The comparison in @eq-intro-self-ref may favor the model's performance relative to that in @eq-intro-latent-ref: the bias term $b_A$ cancels from the model $\widehat Y_A$'s error, accumulating to the human annotator $Y_B$'s error.

Aside from the analysis above, previous work has also shown that models can learn systematic tendencies in how individual annotators label data [@binns2017like; @geva2019we; @nichyporuk2022rethinking]. A reported model advantage may therefore reflect, in part, agreement with the reference's annotation patterns. However, several questions remain open, particularly in real-world medical applications:

- **To what extent does annotation bias affect model–human comparisons?**
- **Could accounting for this bias reverse the conclusion?**
- **How can we identify an annotator whose labels can serve as a reliable reference for such comparisons?**

To address these questions, we focus on predicting thoracic abnormalities from chest X-rays using the VinDr-CXR dataset [@PhysioNet-vindr-cxr-1.0.0; @nguyen2022vindr], accessed through PhysioNet [@pollard_physionet_2026], which provides independent annotations from multiple radiologists for the same images. We train models on individual radiologists' labels and compare their performance with that of other radiologists under different evaluation references. This setting allows us to examine how the choice of training annotator and evaluation reference affects the conclusions of model–human comparisons.

The article proceeds in three parts. [Part I](#part-1) formulates annotation bias and develops a statistical test for whether using the training annotator as the evaluation reference favors the model, supported by experiments on VinDr-CXR. In [part II](#part-2), we consider scores obtained by aggregating binary labels across abnormality categories, and develop a statistical test to assess whether a reference annotator is reliable for the model–human performance comparison. [Part III](#part-3) extends the analysis to binary abnormality labels using a Bernoulli formulation.

<!-- Human labels enter a model twice: first as a training signal, and later as the standard against which its predictions are judged. These roles are often discussed separately. Their interaction matters when annotators differ systematically. -->

Such findings must be interpreted together with the reference and metric used. ## Conclusion {#conclusion}

A model–human comparison is also a comparison of how the model and human relate to an evaluation reference. When the model learns one annotator's systematic tendencies, using that annotator as the reference can change its apparent advantage. Task I makes that shift measurable. In the real scalar experiment, four of six configurations show a significant positive self-reference effect, while the two configurations trained on R10 have negative estimated effects. For the 27 binary findings, the effect is significant at nominal α = 0.05 in 29 of the 162 finding-level tests, against about 8 expected by chance.

Task II asks a different question: can the reference preserve the direction of the comparison against a specified latent target? The central idea is to compare a lower bound on the strength of the observed gap with an upper bound on the change caused by replacing the latent target with the reference. Trained annotator models make this approach usable with sparse labeling overlap, while introducing assumptions about their own errors. The continuous procedure is a Gaussian working-model analysis; its observed certification frequency should be read in that light.

Binary labels reveal why averaging alone is not enough. Centering annotator biases on the logit scale need not center their probabilities. Larger panels reduce random fluctuations, but a curvature-related component remains in the bound. The semi-synthetic results show how additional references can nevertheless make the certification rule substantially less restrictive in the evaluated settings.

The practical lesson is to specify the reference, the comparison target, and the uncertainty together. A detected self-reference effect is not a verdict about which annotator is correct. A certificate is a comparison-specific conclusion under explicit assumptions. Keeping those distinctions visible makes claims about model–human performance easier to interpret and harder to overstate.

<script>
// Local preview only: reload when the rendered page changes on disk.
// Quarto's own preview reload does not fire reliably here; this checks the
// served page once a second and reloads after it has settled on a new version.
(function () {
  var host = location.hostname;
  if (location.protocol !== "http:" || (host !== "localhost" && host !== "127.0.0.1")) return;
  var baseline = null;
  var candidate = null;
  var KEY = "ab-preview-state";

  // Remember the open Part and the scroll position across a preview reload.
  function activeTab() {
    var panes = document.querySelectorAll("#research-parts > .tab-content > .tab-pane");
    for (var i = 0; i < panes.length; i++) if (panes[i].classList.contains("active")) return i;
    return 0;
  }
  function saveAndReload() {
    try { sessionStorage.setItem(KEY, JSON.stringify({ tab: activeTab(), y: window.pageYOffset })); } catch (e) {}
    location.reload();
  }
  var saved = null;
  try { saved = JSON.parse(sessionStorage.getItem(KEY) || "null"); sessionStorage.removeItem(KEY); } catch (e) {}
  if (saved) {
    if ("scrollRestoration" in history) history.scrollRestoration = "manual";
    window.addEventListener("load", function () {
      var btn = document.querySelectorAll('#research-parts > ul.nav-tabs [data-bs-toggle="tab"]')[saved.tab];
      if (btn && window.bootstrap && window.bootstrap.Tab) window.bootstrap.Tab.getOrCreateInstance(btn).show();
      function restore() { window.scrollTo(0, saved.y); }
      restore();
      [100, 500, 1200].forEach(function (t) { setTimeout(restore, t); });
    });
  }

  function digest(text) {
    var h = 0;
    for (var i = 0; i < text.length; i++) h = (h * 31 + text.charCodeAt(i)) | 0;
    return text.length + ":" + h;
  }
  function check() {
    fetch(location.pathname, { cache: "no-store" })
      .then(function (r) { return r.ok ? r.text() : null; })
      .then(function (text) {
        if (text === null) return;
        var d = digest(text);
        if (baseline === null || d === baseline) { baseline = baseline || d; candidate = null; return; }
        if (d === candidate) { saveAndReload(); } else { candidate = d; }
      })
      .catch(function () {})
      .then(function () { setTimeout(check, 1000); });
  }
  setTimeout(check, 1000);
})();
</script>
